## Assigned Readings

- Title: **Publish your computer code, it is good enough**
- Author(s): Nick Barnes
- Year: 2011
- Journal: Nature 467, 753
- <doi:10.1038/467753a>

\

- Title: **Top ten reasons to not share your code (and why you should anyway)**
- Author(s): Randall LeVeque
- Year: 2012
- Journal: Software Sustainability Institute
- <https://faculty.washington.edu/rjl/pubs/topten/topten.pdf>



## Reflections

::: {.callout-note title="bCourses Submission"}
Submit your answers---to the following questions---to the corresponding 
assignment in bCourses.

Accepted formats: PDF, HTML, MS Word (`.docx`), or Google Doc
:::


## Reflection 1

- Open a script or software pipeline you built just a year ago. 

- If you were forced to post that exact file publicly on GitHub right now, "as is," 
would you feel absolute panic or deep embarrassment regarding your programming skills?

- What would be the primary reason for your hesitation to share your code?


## Reflection 2

- Put yourself in the shoes of a busy researcher managing multiple projects.

- If a stranger downloads your public GitHub repository and emails you a list of 
things they don't understand, where do you draw the personal boundary?

- How do you separate your duty to provide scientific transparency 
(the code works for the paper) from your right to protect your personal time 
from being hijacked by outside users demanding free tech support?


## Reflection 3

- Think about a script or software pipeline you built months ago.

- If the software environment inevitably breaks, why does simply allowing an 
outside reviewer to **read** your raw, un-runnable text logic still hold scientific value?


## Rubric

::: {.callout-important}
Generic responses that do not mention a specific 
past assignment name or unique piece of code from your own experience will 
receive a score of zero.
:::

- **Full Credit (5 Points)**: Response is highly specific, names unique personal 
or localized constraints, and explicitly connects the personal experience 
back to the prompt in each question. Clearly written by a human.

- **Partial Credit (2-3 Points)**: Response is correct but uses vague or generic 
examples (e.g., "I lost a file once" instead of naming the script). Sounds like 
a generic summary an AI could have written.

- **No Credit (0 Points)**: Response relies entirely on abstract definitions, 
fails to provide personal context, or uses copy-pasted text from a webpage
or AI tool.
